messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Interpreting RJMCMC
parts:
Hello all,

This isn't necessarily a NIMBLE question and I'm happy to be referred elsewhere. I'm curious about interpretation of RJMCMC. Below are a few thoughts/questions I have.

It seems that coefficients get toggled to 0 when indicator variables toggle to 0. I've thus made summary statistics of the non-0 values of coefficients, in addition to summarising the proportion of iterations in which the RJMCMC included the covariate. However, one could get a coefficient that doesn't overlap 0 ('significant') of a rarely included covariate (I have one example where the inclusion was 0.14). What would be the best way to report RJMCMC results? Can anyone point me to any literature on how to report results? Is there a 'significant' level of RJMCMC inclusion probability?

Kind regards,
Matt

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting RJMCMC
parts:
Matt, I'm sorry I don't have a reference to point you to, but the general way(s) that I've reported results (for model parameter theta subject to RJMCMC) in these situations roughly follows:

1) Conditional posterior summary statistics of theta.  Providing the BCI and posterior mean/median/etc of theta, using the iterations when theta is non-zero (included in the model), so this is the conditional posterior distribution p(theta | data, theta in the model).

2) Unconditional posterior summary statistics of theta.  Providing the BCI and posterior mean/median/etc of theta, using all MCMC iterations (those where theta = 0, and where theta is non-zero), so this is the posterior distribution p(theta | data).

3) As you suggested, reporting the proportion of MCMC iterations in which theta is non-zero (included in the model), so this is p(theta is in the model).  I don't know of any standard "threshold" against which to compare this proportion.

I know this is un-supported by references, but these are things I've reported in the past.

Hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting RJMCMC
parts:
Some good leads might be found in Hooten and Hobbs (2015, https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0661.1)  the King et al. 2010 book (https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~rking33/Book-website/index.html), and/or Johnson and Hoeting 2011 (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0025677).  
-Perry
P.S. Thanks to Sally for these ideas as well.
